brief.audience: DBA5103 mining teammates and project assessor
brief.job: Compare the three mining cases and provide a constraint-first, code-mapped audit dictionary.
brief.narrative: Comparison first, mechanism and schedules second, strategy evidence and limitations third.
required_facts: Day 75 earliest target for full resources; constrained cases unreachable in Year 1

All parameter dictionary keys and public solver controls categorized
All seven compact solver variable families have domains and annual counts
Decision variables, fixed coefficients, expressions and CSV outputs distinguished

content.title: Mining strategy under three resource budgets
content.subtitle: Three-case comparison | Constraint audit reference: pages 4-8
content.author: Jiahe | DBA5103 Mining Module

summary.claim: All three Year 1 optima buy Copper, buy Steel, and farm Zone 2. Resource budgets change when that strategy becomes affordable and how much it earns.
takeaways: Full resources: earliest target Day 75; 177,440.85g at Day 112.
90 to 134 energy: year-end cash rises from 26,946.02g to 80,467.45g.
Copper and Steel pay back; buying Gold immediately reduces cash.

chapters.title: Budgets change the outcome, not the upgrade sequence
chapters.claim: All three Year 1 optima buy Copper, buy Steel, and farm Zone 2. Resource budgets change when that strategy becomes affordable and how much it earns.
paragraphs: Case A uses all resources. Case B reserves one third of energy, time and starting cash. Case C raises only energy from 90 to 134; its 300 minutes and one third of 500g remain unchanged. Case C is an energy sensitivity, not an equal split.

All cases retain the 100,000g target, mine opening on Day 5, two-day submission lockout, expected yields and a partial final floor. Other-activity income is excluded; unused daily resources cannot be carried forward.

chapters.title: Clearing one floor unlocks faster growth
chapters.claim: The minimum for the first floor is 132 energy for ordinary rocks, or 133.65776 including the expected gems collected by the compact model. A whole-number budget of 134 removes the early progression barrier.
paragraphs: The first floor requires 33 ordinary rocks. With Basic, each rock needs two swings and every swing costs two energy: the rocks alone therefore need 132 energy. Expected gems add 1.65776 energy. The model can clear a first floor at 133.65776, but not at 133.65766; 134 is the smallest whole-number budget covering the full bundle.

At 90 energy, the Basic pickaxe cannot clear a floor. The player repeatedly harvests a partial first floor until Copper is affordable on Day 36; Zone 2 is delayed until Day 76. At 134 energy, Basic clears one floor per day, Copper arrives on Day 27 and Zone 2 opens on Day 37. After Steel on Day 43, the plan farms Zone 2 from Day 45 for about 1,180.51g per day.

Time remains slack: peak daily mining time is 263.38 of 900 minutes in Case A, 92.19 of 300 in Case B, and 138.99 of 300 in Case C. The added energy accelerates progression and cash generation; more time alone would not remove the initial rock-clearance barrier.

figure.caption: Crossing the first-floor energy threshold lifts year-end cash by 53,521.43g, with time and starting cash held fixed.

chapters.title: Upgrade promptly when it pays back
chapters.claim: With enough time to recover the investment, buy Copper and Steel as soon as affordable, unlock and repeatedly farm Zone 2, and skip Gold unless deeper progression is required.
paragraphs: In all three Year 1 plans, Copper and Steel are submitted on their first affordable morning. Delaying one purchase by a day lowers cash after reoptimization; these tests do not prove that every later date is worse.

Gold lowers cash when forced on its first affordable morning. The short-horizon exception also matters: the full-resource Day-28 optimum skips Steel, and both constrained Day-28 plans buy no upgrades.

Strict full clearance deadlocks Case B at 166.67g. Case C stays feasible: Copper on Day 27, Steel on Day 48, and 53,391.54g at Day 112. One-day submission lockout also preserves Copper, Steel and Zone 2 in all cases. These are tested patterns, not a universal theorem.

chapters.title: Start with the constraint checklist
chapters.claim: Check the coded constraints against the agreed rules. Solver optimality is not a certificate that the game has been modeled correctly.
paragraphs: Scope: XT0006 is the compact Year 1 model behind this report; XT0005 supplies data and an explicit Spring formulation. See page 8 for the variable crosswalk.

OPEN C03: at T=28, forced Day 21 allows Zone 1 clears=2, marginal entry=1 and marginal rocks=8, plus Zone 2 clears=1 (11,079.59g). OneMarg does not prevent an uncleared shallower floor before a deeper clear. Repair and rerun before claiming full route equivalence. The three selected annual plans did not show this pattern.

chapters.title: Separate budgets, rules and run settings
chapters.claim: These inputs are fixed before solving. Distinguish game data, scenario choices and numerical controls when checking a constraint.
paragraphs: Units: gold coins (g), game minutes, energy, rocks and floors. Initial cash is unrounded internally; sharing resources does not reduce prices or upgrade costs.
Caps 4/5 and M_energy=600 need rechecking if energy rises or food is added. Base T=112 has 1842 rows; MinMarg adds 324 and Time adds 432, potentially exceeding the 2000-row license.

Physics: 2 energy per swing; 1.4 minutes per swing or container. Loader constants; compare S6/S8.

chapters.title: Trace profile inputs to their sources
chapters.claim: Revenue and resource use depend on the same capacities, hit requirements and prices. Check their source arithmetic before interpreting the solution.
paragraphs: Historical names: mine_1_40 covers floors 1-39; mine_41_80 covers 40-79; mine_81_120 covers 80-120. Do not infer boundaries from these identifiers.
Compact model: collect all expected gems and containers on entered floors. XT0005 allows optional collection; agree which rule to use before integration.

chapters.title: Distinguish decisions from expressions
chapters.claim: Year 1 has 108 active days and 15 scalar decisions per day: 1620 columns, comprising 864 binary and 756 general integer variables in the report.
paragraphs: Counts refer to XT0006 with integer_rocks=True. No decisions exist before Day 5; fixing upgrade dates changes bounds, not column counts. Counts were checked from Gurobi.
Expressions reuse decisions without adding columns. p_expr is a tool state; p_push_z1 is a progression decision; params is the fixed input dictionary. These names represent different objects.

chapters.title: Keep CSV outputs out of the decision list
chapters.claim: CSV columns describe a solved plan. Treating outputs as fresh decisions or inventory can double-count cash, material and state during integration.
paragraphs: Confirm partial floors, mandatory gem collection, upgrade timing, cash-equivalent costs and C03 ordering. Before aggregation, filter Scenario, Objective and Horizon.

Integration needs one shared cash balance and energy/time budgets, with agreed transaction timing. If physical materials are introduced, replace immediate sales consistently; never spend gross Cum_* production twice.
